Let [MATH: V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]] be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on [MATH: \left[0,1\right],] equipped with the inner product

[MATH: \langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.]

Calculate the norm of the vector [MATH: f(t)= 2t-1.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The norm of a vector [MATH: f(t)] with respect to an inner product [MATH: \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle] is defined as

[MATH: \| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle f(t), f(t) \rangle}.]

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

[MATH: ⟨f(t), f(t)⟩|= ∫_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(2t − 1)^{2}dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(4t^{2} − 4t + 1)dt; = ((4t^{3})/(3) − 2t^{2} + t)|_{0}^{1}; = (4)/(3) − 2 + 1; = (1)/(3)]

Therefore,

[MATH: \| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Any vector space [MATH: V] combined with an inner product [MATH: \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle] on [MATH: V] is called an inner product space.

Content:
When referring to inner product spaces, we often say that the vector space [MATH: V] is equipped with the inner product [MATH: \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.]

Content:
The norm of a vector [MATH: \mathbf v\in V] in an inner product space is defined as

Content:
[MATH: ‖v‖ = sqrt(⟨v, v⟩).]

Content:
This definition allows us to apply the geometric concept of length to vectors defined in abstract vector spaces. This is because the norm of a vector [MATH: \mathbf v] in an inner product space is a generalization of the norm (or length) of a vector in Euclidean space. To see this, recall that for [MATH: \mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n,] we have

Content:
[MATH: \Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert = \sqrt{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{x}},]

Content:
and we have already seen that the dot product is itself an inner product.

Content:
Let's consider an example. Suppose that an inner product on [MATH: V = \mathbb{R}^3] defined as

Content:
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = 3x_1 y_1 + 2x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.]
Now consider the vector [MATH: \mathbf v\in V,] given by
[MATH: [1; 2; 1]]

Content:
Computing [MATH: \|\mathbf{v}\|] using our definition, we get

Content:
[MATH: ‖v‖|= sqrt(⟨v, v⟩); = sqrt(3 ⋅ (1 ⋅ 1) + 2 ⋅ (2 ⋅ 2) + 2 ⋅ (1 ⋅ 1)); = sqrt(3 + 8 + 2); = sqrt(13).]
